oidc_jwt.description: Authorization code flow requests without a nonce may succeed.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not treat absence of nonce in a pure code-flow authorization request as a standalone vulnerability.

oidc_jwt.description: SAML-backed logins do not support refresh tokens and offline_access is ignored.
oidc_jwt.note: Missing refresh_token in SAML flows is by design.

oidc_jwt.description: Authproxy connector does not support refresh tokens.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag absence of refresh tokens for authproxy-backed sessions.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex issues a new refresh token on every refresh by default.
oidc_jwt.note: Old refresh token reuse after a successful refresh is expected to fail and should not be reported as inconsistent session handling.

oidc_jwt.description: Token exchange returns the issued token in access_token regardless of requested_token_type, with the actual type indicated by issued_token_type.
oidc_jwt.note: The executor must treat access_token as the bearer credential even for exchanged tokens of varying logical types.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex can intentionally issue an ID token whose aud is a different client than the one that initiated login when audience:server:client_id scope is used and the target client trusts the requester via trustedPeers.
oidc_jwt.source: custom-scopes-claims-clients.md: Cross-client trust and authorized party
oidc_jwt.note: This is an explicit feature, not audience-confusion, when trustedPeers is configured.

oidc_jwt.description: Public clients without explicit redirectURIs only allow localhost or urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob redirects.
oidc_jwt.note: Redirect URI rejection for other values is expected behavior, not a flow-coherence bug.

oidc_jwt.description: SAML connector ignores offline_access and does not support refresh tokens.
oidc_jwt.note: Absence of refresh_token for SAML-backed logins is by design.

oidc_jwt.description: For upstream OIDC connectors, groups claims only refresh when the ID token is refreshed; regular refresh flow does not update groups.
oidc_jwt.note: Stale groups across ordinary refresh behavior are documented and should not be treated as a cache-coherence vulnerability unless the test specifically refreshes the upstream ID token.

oidc_jwt.description: When getUserInfo is enabled on an upstream OIDC connector, UserInfo claims take priority over claims returned by the ID token.
oidc_jwt.note: Differences between upstream ID token claims and final Dex claims may be by design because UserInfo overrides ID token values.

oidc_jwt.constraint: Dex dynamic management APIs are gRPC-only. The documentation explicitly states v2's API is entirely gRPC and not REST/gRPC-gateway. Do NOT invent REST admin endpoints such as enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_application, update_application, or cleanup_auth_method from these docs.

For I1 issuer-validation tests against Dex as an upstream-token consumer in token exchange, configure the OIDC connector issuer explicitly. The submitted subject token is verified against the connector's configured issuer; without a distinct issuer configuration, trust-anchor substitution and issuer-mismatch tests are not meaningful.

For I1 audience-binding tests on Dex token exchange, use a control token whose aud matches the intended upstream client and an attack token whose aud targets a different client/provider. Dex documentation for OIDC and OIDC Core implies audience is a required validation dimension; without a control login, rejection may be misread as generic upstream-token invalidity.

For I2 freshness tests on Dex-issued tokens, use the token response field expires_in and the documented expiry settings rather than assuming fixed lifetimes. Dex token lifetimes are configurable under expiry.idTokens, authRequests, and refreshTokens.

Numeric sentinel analysis: Dex duration settings are configured as explicit duration strings (number + unit such as 10m, 6h). The provided docs do not define 0 or -1 sentinel semantics for expiry or rotation settings. Do NOT assume 0 disables expiry or that -1 means strict/disabled.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against upstream OIDC token exchange, include a CONTROL exchange using a valid upstream token alongside the ATTACK token. Otherwise a failed exchange cannot be distinguished from broken connector configuration, missing getUserInfo for access tokens, or bad client authentication.

Dex token exchange currently supports only the OIDC connector. Do NOT attempt oidc_jwt token-exchange tests through OAuth, SAML, LDAP, or other connector types; failures there are setup errors, not security findings.

When exchanging upstream access tokens rather than ID tokens, set the OIDC connector getUserInfo=true if you expect Dex to validate/access claims from access tokens. The docs state getUserInfo is required if you want to exchange from access tokens to Dex-issued tokens.

For I5 scope-escalation tests on token exchange, request only documented Dex scopes: openid, email, profile, groups, federated:id, offline_access, and audience:server:client_id:(client-id). Claims beyond requested scopes may be absent by design, so compare exchanged-token claims only against the requested scope set.

For I5 cross-client audience tests, use Dex's dynamic audience scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id) only when the target client explicitly trusts the requesting client via trustedPeers. Without trustedPeers, rejection is by design and not an audience-validation bug.

For I3 default-behavior tests, remember Dex enables authorization_code, refresh_token, and token-exchange grant types by default when grantTypes is omitted. A test that expects token exchange to be disabled must explicitly configure grantTypes to exclude it.

For OIDC request-object tests (I1 oidc_request_object_alg_none), Dex certification notes indicate unsigned request objects may be either supported correctly or rejected as unsupported. Treat explicit rejection/unsupported behavior as non-vulnerable; only acceptance of attacker-controlled unsigned request parameters is a finding.

For OIDC code-flow nonce tests, Dex certification results note that code flow without nonce succeeds. Do NOT flag missing nonce in pure authorization-code requests as a vulnerability by itself; nonce is strongly relevant to ID token replay in browser flows, but Dex may accept code flow requests without it by design.

For OIDC callback coherence tests (I3 state_swap, code_injection, redirect_uri_mismatch), the valid oracle is token-endpoint success vs failure for the same code-flow transaction. Dex docs emphasize state links the user who started the flow to the one who finished it and prevents replay; do not infer identity bugs from UI redirects alone.

For token exchange client authentication, include client credentials via HTTP Basic authentication as documented. Rejections caused by missing Basic auth are setup failures, not token-validation findings.

Dex documentation describes dynamic management through a gRPC API, not documented REST admin endpoints. Do NOT assume REST endpoints for enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_auth_role, create_policy, revoke_session, cleanup_auth_method, create_application, or user CRUD from these docs.
The OIDC discovery document explicitly exposes authorization_endpoint=/auth and token_endpoint=/token. Use these exact paths for OIDC flows.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against Dex-issued tokens, include a CONTROL flow that obtains a valid token first. Otherwise a failed attack flow may reflect bad client setup, connector choice, or disabled grant type rather than freshness enforcement.

For I3 state_swap and code_injection tests, the sequence MUST preserve the original state value and callback session binding. Dex documentation states the client must verify state to ensure the user who started the flow is the one who finished it and to prevent replay.

For I3 redirect_uri_mismatch tests, the token request to /token MUST use the same redirect_uri used at /auth. Dex documents standard authorization code flow semantics and registered redirect URIs; mismatches should be tested as flow-binding failures, not identity mismatches.

For OIDC request object tests (alg_none, request tampering), Dex certification results indicate unsigned request objects may be either supported correctly or rejected as unsupported. Treat rejection as acceptable behavior; only acceptance with altered semantics is a finding.

For PKCE-related tests, Dex certification shows valid PKCE succeeds, but the docs do not state PKCE is mandatory for all clients. Do NOT treat lack of universal PKCE enforcement as an identity-binding bug unless the same code can be redeemed without any client binding.
For token_exchange tests, include connector_id in the /token request. Dex requires connector_id in addition to RFC 8693 parameters; omitting it causes setup failure rather than a security rejection.

For token_exchange using upstream access tokens, configure the upstream OIDC connector with getUserInfo=true if claims must be derived from access tokens. Without getUserInfo, access tokens may be treated as opaque and tests can fail for setup reasons.

For cross-provider JWT audience and trust-anchor substitution tests on upstream OIDC token exchange, configure the connector issuer exactly. Dex docs state issuer MUST match provider discovery, with issuerAlias only for off-spec providers. A mismatched issuer setup invalidates the test.

For I1 issuer-validation tests on upstream OIDC connectors, the configured issuer is an exact string match against discovery metadata. Do NOT use wildcard or pattern values; if multiple issuers must be accepted, create separate connector configurations rather than attempting a wildcard.

For I5 audience tests on Dex-issued ID tokens, use the dynamic scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id) only when the target client explicitly lists the requesting client in trustedPeers. Otherwise rejection is by design.

For I5 scope-escalation tests, remember Dex scopes directly control which claims appear in issued tokens: email, profile, groups, federated:id, offline_access, and dynamic audience scopes. Missing claims outside requested scope are by design, not authorization failures.

For I5 group-policy style tests using upstream OIDC connectors, groups claims are disabled by default unless insecureEnableGroups=true on the connector. If groups are absent without that setting, do NOT interpret the result as claim stripping or policy enforcement.

For freshness tests involving refresh tokens, Dex rotates refresh tokens on every refresh by default. Reuse of an old refresh token after a successful refresh may fail by design due to rotation, not because of broader replay protection on access or ID tokens.

Numeric sentinel analysis: Dex token expiry settings are documented as explicit durations in the form number+unit (s,m,h). The provided docs do not define 0 or -1 sentinel meanings for expiry, leeway, or reuse parameters. Do NOT assume 0 disables validation or means unlimited; treat unspecified values as implementation defaults outside the documented API surface.

Dex does not document REST admin endpoints for enabling auth methods, configuring JWT/OIDC connectors, creating roles, policies, users, applications, or revoking sessions. Dynamic management is via gRPC API, not HTTP REST. The fuzzer MUST treat these canonical setup operations as absent for Dex REST extraction and rely only on documented OIDC endpoints for oidc_jwt.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against Dex as an OIDC provider, the sequence MUST include a control authorization-code or token-exchange request using a valid token/time window. Without a control, a failed login/token exchange cannot be distinguished from bad client configuration, missing connector_id, or disabled grant type.

Dex token exchange works only with the OIDC connector. The fuzzer MUST configure and target an OIDC upstream connector for oidc_jwt token-exchange tests; other connector types are out of scope and will fail by design.

For token_exchange, Dex requires the upstream connector to be specified with connector_id and requires client credentials via HTTP Basic Authentication even when the client is marked public. The fuzzer MUST send connector_id and client credentials; otherwise failures are setup errors, not security rejections.

For access-token subject_token exchanges, Dex documentation states getUserInfo is required if you want to exchange from access tokens to Dex-issued tokens. The fuzzer MUST enable getUserInfo when subject_token_type is access_token; otherwise rejection is by design and not an I1/I5 finding.

Dex token exchange returns the issued token in access_token regardless of requested_token_type, with the actual type indicated by issued_token_type. The fuzzer MUST treat access_token as the credential field and MUST NOT expect an id_token field from token exchange.

Dex-issued tokens are bound to clients. For I5 audience and cross-client tests, the fuzzer MUST vary client_id and requested scopes deliberately and inspect aud/azp in the resulting token rather than assuming tokens are client-agnostic.

Cross-client audience issuance in Dex is by design when the requested scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id) is used and the target client explicitly lists the requesting client in trustedPeers. The fuzzer MUST NOT flag aud != requesting client_id as an I5 violation unless trustedPeers was not configured.

For I3 jwt_default_role_change-style coherence analogs on Dex, config changes to clients/connectors between separate authorization requests are by design. A valid coherence test must show inconsistent handling of the same request/session state, not merely that a later request follows updated configuration.

Dex authorization endpoint supports code flow without nonce, and certification results explicitly note request-without-nonce succeeds for code flow. The fuzzer MUST NOT report missing nonce in pure authorization-code requests as an I2 bug for Dex OP behavior.

For OIDC request object alg_none testing, Dex certification notes unsigned request objects may be supported correctly or rejected as unsupported. The fuzzer MUST treat either explicit rejection or standards-compliant handling as non-vulnerable unless unsigned request objects are accepted and security-sensitive parameters are honored unexpectedly.
Dex supports PKCE validation in code flow. For PKCE-related I3 tests, the oracle should assert token endpoint rejection/non-200 on invalid or missing verifier cases rather than comparing identities.

Dex refresh tokens are rotated on every refresh by default. The fuzzer MUST use the newest refresh token after each refresh and MUST NOT treat reuse of an older refresh token as a replay vulnerability if it is rejected.

Numeric sentinel analysis: Dex token settings document no special sentinel values such as 0 or -1 for expiry/rotation fields in the provided docs. Durations must be explicit strings with time units (for example 10m, 6h). The fuzzer MUST NOT assume 0 disables or defaults any token validation behavior.
